nameStory: The Latticed Sheet-web Weaver gets its name from the intricate, geometric pattern of its flat web that resembles old-fashioned lattice work on garden trellises. The word 'latticed' comes from the French 'lattis,' meaning a framework of crossed strips, which perfectly describes how this spider's silk creates a delicate, mesh-like sheet.
description: The Latticed Sheet-web Weaver is a tiny spider that creates flat, horizontal webs close to the ground or stretched between low vegetation. These diminutive arachnids are part of the sheet weaver family, known for their paper-thin webs that look like miniature trampolines. They're quite small, typically measuring just a few millimeters in body length, making them easy to overlook despite their intricate craftsmanship. You're more likely to notice their delicate webs glistening with morning dew than spot the spider itself.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates a flat, horizontal sheet web with a fine mesh pattern that feels papery-thin to the touch and often sparkles with dewdrops in morning light

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small body, just a few millimeters long - about the size of a pinky nail or smaller, making them barely visible without close inspection

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Hangs upside down beneath their sheet web, quickly running across the silk surface when disturbed with a distinctive scurrying motion

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rounded abdomen with relatively long, thin legs that appear delicate and almost translucent in bright light

idTips.label: Web Placement
idTips.description: Webs are positioned low to the ground, often stretched between grass stems or small shrubs, rarely more than a foot above soil level

habitat: Look for Latticed Sheet-web Weavers in areas with dense, low vegetation like meadows, forest edges, and gardens where their webs can stretch between grass stems and small plants. They prefer somewhat moist environments with good cover, often found in areas that receive morning dew. Their webs are typically positioned within a foot of the ground in protected spots among vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to construct their characteristic sheet webs in areas with emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when webs are most visible and spiders are actively hunting. Morning dew makes their webs particularly noticeable during this season.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and egg sacs are produced. Webs may become less maintained as spiders focus on reproduction before winter.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, with the species overwintering in egg form or as juveniles hidden in protected locations under leaf litter.

funFact: Despite being found across multiple continents from North America to Japan, this tiny spider was likely spread around the world accidentally by human trade - it's become one of the most cosmopolitan spiders on Earth, yet most people have never noticed it!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small sheet web spiders in the same family, but the Latticed Sheet-web Weaver's web has a distinctly fine, regular mesh pattern. Memory trick: Think 'lattice fence' - their webs look like tiny, delicate garden lattice work stretched horizontally.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'clathrata' comes from Latin meaning 'latticed' or 'barred,' directly referencing the geometric pattern of their webs. This species is part of the Linyphiidae family, often called 'money spiders' in some regions due to folklore that finding one brings good luck.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Filmy Dome Spider, the Latticed Sheet-web Weaver creates flat sheet webs rather than dome-shaped ones. While the Old World Dome Sheetweaver also makes structured webs, the Latticed Sheet-web Weaver's mesh pattern is more regular and geometric. All three species are tiny, but web architecture is the key distinguishing feature between them.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relative the Latticed Sheet-web Weaver which builds flat, horizontal webs with visible lattice patterns, the Filmy Dome Spider's web is distinctly three-dimensional and smooth.
Compared to its relatives the Filmy Dome Spider and Latticed Sheet-web Weaver, the Old World Dome Sheetweaver is distinguished by its heavily banded yellow-brown legs with numerous dark rings.
